title: How much paper does the net of this cuboid use?
description: A cuboid has sides of four, two and one centimetres. The board lists the three pairs of rectangles, lays the four walls in a row, joins the top and bottom, and adds the six areas. Keeko's doubt is that multiplying the three lengths gives the area.
teaching_notes: One idea: a cuboid has three pairs of equal rectangles, and the area of the net is twice the sum of the three different rectangles. Watch for students who multiply all three lengths and get the space inside instead.

source: Draw a net of a cuboid 4 cm by 2 cm by 1 cm and find the are
video_script.why: The child draws the net of a cuboid from its three pairs of equal rectangles and finds its area, because the net is made of all six faces.
video_script.substitution: cuboid 4 cm by 2 cm by 1 cm; rectangles 4 by 2, 4 by 1, 2 by 1, two of each; walls in a row 4, 2, 4, 2 long and 1 cm tall.
video_script.anchor: the cuboid of the book unfolded into a net of six rectangles
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko multiplies the three lengths to get the area; that number measures the space inside the cuboid, not the faces, so the doubt is struck.
video_script.payoff_line: The net is six rectangles with area twenty eight square centimetres

final_answer.value: A net of six rectangles with area 28 square cm
final_answer.spoken: a net of six rectangles with area twenty eight square centimetres

maths_rules: cuboid 4 cm by 2 cm by 1 cm has 6 faces in 3 equal pairs
row of walls: 4, 2, 4, 2 long, all 1 cm tall; the row is 4 + 2 + 4 + 2 = 12 cm long, which is the distance round a 4 by 2 base
area of net = 2 x (8 + 4 + 2) = 2 x 14 = 28 square cm
wrong idea: 4 x 2 x 1 = 8 measures the space inside, not the faces
video_script.design: One idea: three pairs of equal rectangles. The walls sit in a row, the top and bottom join to one wall, and each pair glows in its own colour as it is counted.

narration: <bookmark mark='six'/>A cuboid has six faces, and every face is a rectangle.
<bookmark mark='pairs'/>Opposite faces are equal, so the six faces make three equal pairs.
<bookmark mark='area'/>The area of the net is the area of all six faces together.

narration: <bookmark mark='list'/>Step one, list the rectangles, because opposite faces are equal. We need two of four by two, two of four by one, and two of two by one.

beats.on_screen: Step 2: four walls in a row: 4 by 1, 2 by 1, 4 by 1, 2 by 1, all 1 cm tall

narration: <bookmark mark='row'/>Step two, draw the four walls in a row, as they go round the base. They are four, two, four and two long.
<bookmark mark='tall'/>Every wall is one centimetre tall.

narration: <bookmark mark='areas'/>Step four, add the area of each kind of rectangle. Four times two is eight, four times one is four, and two times one is two.
<bookmark mark='twice'/>Every kind appears twice. The area is two times the sum of eight, four and two.

beats.on_screen: Answer: a net of six rectangles with area 28 square cm
narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>The net is six rectangles with area twenty eight square centimetres.

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks we should multiply four, two and one to get the area.
